claims.text: The starting coating has a dual FCC/BCC microstructure.
The starting coating has a relatively uniform grain-size distribution and minimal initial precipitate formation.
Controlled thermal aging will promote nucleation and growth of nanoscale precipitates along FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
The untreated baseline will have less pronounced precipitate formation than the thermally aged coating.
Nanoscale precipitates at FCC/BCC interfaces enhance creep resistance.
Interfacial nanoscale precipitates act as grain-boundary pinning sites.
The precipitates inhibit dislocation motion during continuous loading.
The precipitates inhibit grain-boundary sliding during sustained stress.
Blocking dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding limits the accumulation of time-dependent plastic deformation.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit a lower creep strain rate than untreated samples under identical test conditions.
Thermally aged samples will accumulate less total creep deformation than untreated samples.
The proposed comparison is conducted under continuous loading at approximately 0.4–0.6 of the alloy melting temperature.
The mechanism is expected to operate only where temperature promotes precipitate formation without causing substantial grain growth or deleterious phase transformations.
The mechanism is expected to operate only at stresses that induce creep without triggering competing failure modes such as fracture.
Direct evidence linking the formation and stability of FCC/BCC interfacial nanoscale precipitates to creep resistance in the specific alloy system is currently unverified.
